REV. DR. CHARLES WILLIAMS II, SENIOR PASTOR, HISTORIC KING SOLOMON BAPTIST CHURCH: She's the only one in the race that's actually been elected. She was elected a congressperson. She worked in the executive branch.

And of course, she has been a legislator. She understands how to work to get policy passed. Unfortunately, there's nobody else in the race at this time that has that cache.

CORNISH: Historic King Solomon Church. There is always that Black Church vote that comes out, and they aren't always aligned with the academic progressive left vote. We see this in South Carolina. Biden was happy to receive those votes.

Is that the kind of thing that's a wild card here in Michigan, or are those voters also embracing some of these more populist ideas or ideas on foreign policy?

WU: I mean, the strategy that the Stevens campaign is running is to try to run up turnout in Black majority areas in Michigan. Whether that is --

CORNISH: I think I saw her at a church.

WU: Exactly. Right. Right.

CORNISH: The obligatory many times Democrats, Black church visit. That happens.

WU: Exactly. She's been trying to run up turnout there. El-Sayed has been trying to cut into those margins. For example, you know, we saw him going around Detroit with a whole crew of influencers. So it's like it's a much different kind of strategy --

CORNISH: Very different reach, but I understand.

WU: Exactly. MILBANK: And the polling shows him ahead, but it's just sort of a

guess by the pollsters about is it going to be young male white voters? Is it going to be older female black voters? We don't really know until tonight or tomorrow.

CORNISH: Yeah. Both are frustrated for different reasons. And there's always the couch, as it's said, right.

You guys, thank you so much. Hope to have you back in the group.

And tonight, don't miss key primary races across the country, including big gubernatorial and congressional races, as we've talked about of Michigan. We're going to talk about who's going to advance and we're going to have election results all night.

You can get that tonight on CNN and our CNN app.

Next on CNN THIS MORNING, a Republican lawmaker facing censure after an ethics report showing that he gave female staffers jewelry, vacations and guns. But some don't think that punishment goes far enough.

Plus, I'm going to talk to a reporter who sat down with Congressman Max Miller. What he told her about the abuse allegations he's facing.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I know Max. He's a -- he's a good person. I mean, I always thought he was a very good person. And I'm going to let the families figure that out. But it's accusations, and I'm going to let them figure that out.

CORNISH: President Trump publicly standing by embattled Republican Congressman Max Miller, even as his former press secretary launches a new legal battle against Miller.

So, on Monday, Stephanie Grisham's lawyer filed for a temporary restraining order against Miller. Now she's suing him for breaking the terms of a nondisclosure agreement, an agreement that stems from 2021. In a "Washington Post" op-ed, Grisham had written about abuse allegations dealing with an ex-boyfriend, and Miller sued her at the time, but they settled out of court and agreed not to disparage each other publicly.

Grisham now claims Miller violated the deal in this interview back in June.

REP. MAX MILLER (R-OH): Without question, every allegation should be taken seriously. What should be noted is that allegation came out on the same day as somebody's book launch.

And the other part, what I would like to discuss is my ex-wife was with me every single day during that time of my life, in that election. And she, in her own words, will tell you that I never did any of those things. And she never saw evidence of me ever doing those things. And that was nothing more than somebody trying to get notoriety.

CORNISH: Joining the group chat, Harri Leigh, political correspondent at Spectrum News. She conducted that interview with Congressman Miller.

This is a fascinating conversation that you got to have with him. Before we get to the allegations within his family and ex-wife, can you talk about this issue with Stephanie Grisham, why they are all of a sudden back in court?

HARRI LEIGH, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT, SPECTRUM NEWS: Well, they're back in court partly because of that interview and their nondisclosure agreement back in 2021. It appears this was a confidential agreement. So we didn't know until she filed this suit.

But it appears that they agreed not to disparage each other. And she's saying that in that interview, by denying the claims that she made, as well as the claims by his now ex-wife, that he broke that agreement. And as you know, yesterday she also filed a restraining order.

CORNISH: Right. Because he's basically saying there are not multiple allegations, right? He doesn't want this to sound like it's piling up. And so, he reached back to this conversation and she's like, no, keep me out of it.

CORNISH: All right. So, let's talk about the Moreno family. The Senator Bernie Moreno has been obviously, like, very upset and frustrated. He has called for Miller to step down, saying he shouldn't be in Congress anymore.

Joining him, Senator Shelley Moore Capito and Roger Marshall.

Are we going to see any other senators speak up?

ARM: I think Rick Scott might have said something to that effect. Yeah, I don't know.

CORNISH: When does it reach the House? The people who actually work with this guy?

AARON BLAKE, CNN SENIOR POLITICAL REPORER: I think it's getting to that point now. We're seeing signals coming out of the White House where at least Trump is apparently privately saying that he doesn't think Max Miller can win reelection.

That seems like the beginnings of kind of a subtle pressure campaign to convince this person to at least step aside from his reelection campaign. And there's a very good reason for that. You know, even besides from -- aside from kind of the details of the allegations, this is a district that Republicans would worry about losing if Max Miller is on the ballot in November. That's the same with some of these other congressmen, which were talking about.

CORNISH: But now, we're talking about family. So, for instance, Senator Moreno, like I said, he put out a statement where he says, as he admitted privately, Max Miller needs serious psychological help. He's a danger to my daughter. I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter.

And then there is also this audio obtained from earlier this year. Emily Moreno is telling police about an incident on New Year's Eve where she alleged that Miller held a gun to her head when she was changing their infant daughter. So just give you a moment to listen to this.

OFFICER: So when -- when does the gun come into play?

EMILY MORENO, EX-WIFE: When I'm changing (AUDIO DELETED).

OFFICER: And what does he do?

MORENO: Holds it on me.

OFFICER: Holds it on you? Okay, can you show me where he held it to you?

No, hey, it's -- it's okay, that's fine, that's fine. Like I said, I -- that's a hard thing to talk about.

CORNISH: Has he said anything about this incident or others? Because I know he released his own drop box of audio. So, he does want people to kind of hear his side as he's denying these allegations.

LEIGH: Yeah. And I think that's part of the problem is that he keeps releasing more and more information and more evidence that can then be used against him in certain cases. He does deny that this incident even happened.

CORNISH: What does he say about his father in law? Has he talked about what's going on publicly?

LEIGH; So, for a long time he said that they could work together. He said that he could walk and chew gum at the same time. But after a while, he was saying that his father-in-law was helping his daughter, enabling her in what he said was lying. And so that is when he started taking to social media to criticize

him. Bernie Moreno didn't say anything for a very long time. His team consistently said no comment until Sunday, and that is when he released that scathing post on X.

CORNISH: And then he was asked about it. I just want to play some video of the last time Moreno was asked about this incident. Oh, sorry about that. It is actually a full screen. I'm not sure I can say it because it involves swearing.

It says, you know, I hope you never have to go through a situation like this and you wouldn't ask that kind of effing question.

And I think it's a great example of the fact that they do want this not to be so public. This isn't something that they want to be discussed this way. Do you think it would be discussed this way if it weren't two lawmakers involved?

ROCHA: Yeah, I think we'd be having a whole different conversation. We'd also be doing it different if Bernie Moreno wasn't just elected, that means he's not up for reelection. Everybody at home should know. Just because you're a senator don't mean you're up for elections every six years.

Just elected. He's not up for another four and a half years for reelection. But in the house, to your point. Audie, everybody is up every two years. And in this congressional race, it's only an R plus seven, which should be a very safe seat. And in most circumstances, it would be a very safe seat.

But when you put that on the screen, an ad maker like me can run that against -- he's running against an ironworker, a regular union guy, and that makes that be more vulnerable.

That's why you have to put politics in this horrible situation where you're talking about guns and babies, which nobody should live through.

CORNISH: All right, so let's turn to that. Another Huse Republican facing ethics scrutiny. The ethics committee is recommending a full vote to censure North Carolina's Chuck Edwards, a months-long probe found that Edwards engaged in persistent, inappropriate conduct toward two young female staffers. That's from the ethics panel report.

Now, examples that they provided included skipping scheduled house votes to help a staffer decorate her Christmas tree, writing and reading a tearful personal poem at a staffers departure party and buying a staffer lavish gifts, including jewelry worth more than $1,000.

Edwards and his team reject the allegations. They claim that the ethics committee failed to demonstrate that either of the two staffers actually expressed discomfort to Edwards regarding his conduct with them.

The group chat is back. I wanted to follow up with this because just a few weeks ago, Mike

Johnson was saying, I want to ban dating, not just of your own staffers, but across the board. So, obviously, there was like a Houston, we have a problem situation.

What do you see in the fact that there's a censure going on here, but that hasn't come up yet with Moreno.

CORNISH: With Miller. Sorry.

LEIGH: I think that they've -- they've expressed some issues with due process. I think that now that the ethics investigation is over with Edwards, they feel more comfortable moving forward with that. But we have seen several lawmakers refuse to take a stand until the Ethics Committee makes a decision.

I don't actually know if they have started that yet, but --

CORNISH: And I'm going to throw up on screen so people can see the number of lawmakers who are facing some kind of sexual harassment or ethics investigation at this point.

And one of the people in the past was Jorge Santos. And it was interesting. I remember thinking, Jorge Santos is not going to have to leave Congress unless a Democrat also is a problem, and they can be asked to leave Congress. Like there seemed to be a kind of one for one situation that had to happen.

Is that the case right now? Just the balance of power is so tight that leadership is loathe to let anyone go?

ROCHA: That's the point here. I mean, I think that's exactly what's happening.

CORNISH: But even for Democrats, you can be like on your deathbed and still in Congress.

ROCHA: Absolutely. And you can die in office if you stay there until you're 90. I mean, it's just one thing after another.

And I think this is where the American people are fed up with both parties. When you say, what do you think about Democrats? What do you think about Republicans? You're like, well, they're all too old, and they're all a bunch of crooks that seem like they\re acting like a bunch of freaks on Capitol Hill.

ARM: I genuinely weird behavior from Edwards's part.

ARM: From Edwards's part.

ARM: I mean, that's the latest one you've raised, Audie. I just -- it is strange to me that, you know, even if it is true what his office is saying, that none of these people ever complained about this, that one would think it's appropriate to shower young female staffers and these kinds of gifts and invite them to things, it's just, you know, it's strange.

CORNISH: Yeah, which two adult -- two consenting adults outside of this environment? Sure. But you know what I mean? But in Congress, there has been this sense that there's some other standard. And is that dead?

ARM: I think there is some credit that is actually due here to Speaker Johnson, who I would say probably saying nobody who works in Congress can date anybody else who works in Congress is maybe a little bit of an overcorrection. I'm not sure if that's exactly what he proposed, but if it is, I would say that, you know, maybe a bit heavy handed, but look, it's a -- it's a House Republican majority. And that ethics committee is the one that dealt down this decision.

CORNISH: Right, it's Republicans leading that committee. Yeah.

ARM: Edwards. So, you know, I respect the fact and appreciate that there is at least an effort here to clean up house and recognition that there is a problem.

ROCHA: And if Democrats take the House, which they probably will, at least in the house, it'd be interesting to watch how they deal -- how they deal with the ethics committee on either side.

CORNISH: I know, because they also always complain about the ethics committee. That's like a big Democrat thing. They're always frustrated with.

Since you were here, we want to give you something positive to talk about what is in your group chat other than people being like, oh my God, did you talk to this lawmaker? How did that interview go? What are people talking about in your world?

LEIGH: That's been a big thing this week, I'm going to say. But I think, you know, we're talking a lot about how the House, the Senate are going out. They leave so much unfinished business, so much that did not get passed. And it's going to be such a rush when they come back in September. Just talking about the budget, the NDAA, the crypto bill, military funding. So --

CORNISH: The military funding, even?

LEIGH: All the NDAA.

CORNISH: Yeah. You think that's not going to get done this week?

LEIGH: It could, but -- I mean --

CORNISH: Group chats, not hopeful. Okay. Aaron, what about you?

BLAKE: Major League Baseball salary cap. If you look at the trades that happened this week ahead of the trade deadline, the rich get richer. They get all the best players the Dodgers, the Yankees, the Phillies. We're tired of it. The Minnesota Twins need to have a level playing field to be able to compete with those teams. Salary cap.

CORNISH: Really well-delivered. Quite the argument.

ROCHA: And the billionaires.

What's in your group chat?

ROCHA: Look, it's the Latino group chat. We're getting past the primaries, Audie, and we're looking towards the general.

ROCHA: And look at these are great Latino candidates who are up in marginal seats. If Democrats take back Congress, it will be because --

CORNISH: All right. These -- are these folks you're working with?

ROCHA: I've worked with some of these. Randy Villegas, I would draw your attention to who I was talking to in the green room is from Fresno, auto mechanic, college professor. Like working class guy that's not made up.

CORNISH: That this is the other running trend I'm interested in, given ICE and all these things and the miscalculation in the past of left activists about thinking Latinos care about immigration so much, I'm really interested to see.

ROCHA: This story will be the story of the midterms.

ARM: Well, I'm so thrown off because I was going to say the thing about the MLB salary cap.

CORNISH: Also a salary person?

ARM: I'm a Detroit Tigers fan. So, you know, I'm really hurt by this Tarik Skubal situation with Dodgers.

CORNISH: I like this baseball populist.

ARM: But, no, no, no, no, I'm actually going to talk about the new Spider-Man movie because we haven't had a solid superhero movie in a hot minute at this point. And this Spider-Man movie was really quality.

CORNISH: The last one probably was a Spider-Man movie. ARM: Yeah, probably. So, Spider-Man is just like the best pop culture

figure. Honestly, of any --

CORNISH: Certainly the most durable, as is Tom Holland. Yeah.

ARM: So go see it. The world is smaller. It's not huge. There's not like aliens from other dimensions coming in and messing up timelines. So good movie.

CORNISH: Anti-multiverse. What a take. Okay.

ROCHA: Has it already come out? I'm the old guy here. Has Spider-Man come out?

CORNISH: Has already come out. I don't blame you because the hype and run up to these things is just so long.

ROCHA: It's actually show.

CORNISH: No, it's actually out. And it also means both Zendaya and Tom Holland, who may or may not be married, but they probably are, have two top box office films with "The Odyssey" and "Brand New Day". So, shout out to them.

Thanks for being here, guys. Thanks for sharing what's in your group chat?

The headlines are next.

Stevens, El-Sayed Go Head-to-Head in Michigan Primary; Trump: Pirro Folded 'Like an Umbrella' in Pool Vandalism Case. Aired 6-6:30a ET

Aired August 04, 2026 - 06:00   ET

THIS IS A RUSH TRANSCRIPT. THIS COPY MAY NOT BE IN ITS FINAL FORM AND MAY BE UPDATED.

BRAD SMITH, CNN ANCHOR: Some people, as you could see, they could not resist having some fun with it. I mean, let's just take a second and -- yes, there's a little bit of joy than can be found.

Just look at the scene. People are just trying to figure out what is going on. And yes, you've got to play with some bubbles every now and then. It is summertime.

That does it for CNN HEADLINE EXPRESS. I'm Brad Smith. CNN THIS MORNING with Audie Cornish starts right now.

AUDIE CORNISH, CNN ANCHOR: OK. Today in the group chat, a big test for the big tent party. Will voters in Michigan follow other states and go with the far-left candidate, or will the establishment win out?

ABDUL EL-SAYED (D), MICHIGAN SENATORIAL CANDIDATE: Ours is the work of continuously building a bigger movement.

REP. HALEY STEVENS (D-MI), MICHIGAN SENATORIAL CANDIDATE: When it comes to Michigan, I run through anyone and anything to stand up for us.

CORNISH: An embattled congressman refusing to step aside. Now the president weighs in, telling him, quote, "Things aren't looking good." Could this put a red state at risk come November?

And Trump, furious over the Justice Department's decision to drop the Reflecting Pool case. Could Jeanine Pirro be his scapegoat.

And a suspect charged with arson as the wildfires in Washington state rage on this morning. The anguish from residents as they see what was spared from the flames.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: It's a very, very hard loss. All of mine and my siblings' childhood pictures, all the baby clothes, I'm pretty sure my grandpa's ashes, everything was in there.

(END VIDEO CLIP) (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: The energy right now in Detroit and Michigan generally, it's really -- it feels great, you know, a little nerve wracking. But it's a -- it's a lot of people coming in. It almost feels like it's the general election. There's so much energy around it right now.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: In this room --

CORNISH: It is election day in Michigan and a referendum for the Democratic Party. Will voters back the progressive choice or the candidate backed by the establishment?

Good morning, everybody. I'm Audie Cornish, and here is where we start. The most expensive Democratic primary.

After a long and messy campaign today, Democratic voters will decide between congresswoman Haley Stevens or Abdul El-Sayed. Under the big tent, these candidates are on opposite sides. El-Sayed wants Medicare for all. Stevens wants to improve Obamacare.

El-Sayed wants to abolish ICE. Stevens says she backs ICE reforms. And El-Sayed wants to stop aid to Israel. Stevens has been a pro-Israel vote in the House.

It's that last issue that's causing the most division. More than 60 million in cash, pouring in from outside groups to help Stevens. The biggest spender by far: a pro-Israeli super PAC.

STEVENS: There is a reason why Republicans are already spending thousands and thousands of dollars meddling in this primary, trying to maybe get their preferred candidate. Look, when it comes to Michigan, I run through anyone and anything to stand up for us.

EL-SAYED: This movement of ours has proven that it can come through $80 million of spending in lies, because we're willing to hold with us the truth.

You can't buy inspiration. You can't buy people deciding to be a part of something. You can't buy hope. You can't buy belief.

CORNISH: OK. Today in the group chat, Aaron Blake, CNN senior political reporter; Chuck Rocha, Democratic strategist and former senior adviser to Bernie Sanders' presidential campaigns; and Jesse Arm, pollster and vice president at the Manhattan Institute.

Good morning, gentlemen. Welcome to the chat. I want to start with you, Aaron. You were saying Democrats have a new problem as they try to win the Senate. What is that problem? AARON BLAKE, CNN SENIOR POLITICAL REPORTER: Well, what we've seen in

the last several weeks here is the -- the big hurdle that we thought Democrats would have, which would be competing in a lot of these red states. You know, the states that Donald Trump won by double digits.

They've got the polling to back up that they can win in states like Iowa, like Texas, like Ohio. Those are on the table. They need some of those. But even as that happens --

CORNISH: That list is like Iowa, Texas.

CORNISH: Are you sure about this? I'm sort of shocked --

CORNISH: -- shocked to hear these states.

BLAKE: Those are polling pretty competitively.

But at the same time, we've seen these races like Michigan, where we're starting to see some doubts creep in. The Democratic establishment is very concerned, if Abdullah El-Sayed emerges from this primary, that he's going to be a liability in the general election.

And if they're not winning these swing states and these blue states, the map is just very tough for them as far as winning a Democratic Senate majority.

CORNISH: OK. If you live in Michigan, my apologies, because I'm going to play for you some clips from some of the ads you've probably been seeing nonstop from Stevens and El-Sayed. Here we go.

EL-SAYED: Money in your pocket and Medicare --

ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ (D-NY): For all. That's the part they can't stand. That's why billionaires are spending millions to bury Abdul and this movement.

STEVENS: As chief of staff to President Obama's auto rescue, I helped save Michigan jobs.

BARACK OBAMA, FORMER PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: And Haley Stevens, by the way, she was there. She was a critical part of my team.

CORNISH: I love it. The music's giving Michigan Detroit vibes the whole way across the board. Why has this become the proxy battle for the back and forth? Every

time you and I are on set, we talk about like, oh, the Democratic socialists here, the moderates here. What makes Michigan different?

CHUCK ROCHA, DEMOCRATIC STRATEGIST: Well, I think Aaron said it right, is that there's no way for us to win this majority in the Senate unless we can win these Democratic strongholds.

And to your point, what makes Michigan different is that it's supposed to be one that's not this hard to win in November, and it's looking like it could be hard, because the polling just stacks up the way.

There's one thing, Audie, that cuts across all of these that I want to talk about this morning, which is this change electorate. And we've been living through change elections, through lots of elections.

CORNISH: I was about to say, I feel like that's my perennial report.

ROCHA: But let me take that to Michigan. And this is where this Democrat gives Donald Trump credit. Michigan has been so desperate for change, they'd vote for Donald Trump twice. Folks there are sick and tired of being sick and tired, and they're looking for something different.

And I think that's why El-Sayed is doing so well. Sure, he's got a great message and he's got things that may be bad, as well, but a lot more plus than minus. But it's just a change electorate overall.

CORNISH: It's also interesting to see what's going on with donors. "The Wall Street Journal" was reporting that the big, big, like marquee name donors are sitting out; that they've nicknamed the DNC "Do not contribute."

And then, when I look at the cash on hand for Republicans, like, it's super PACs. You know what I mean? Like, it -- it feels like there's been a shift in who spends the money. And obviously, that has to do with the Supreme Court, et cetera.

But are we really feeling it in this election?

JESSE ARM, POLLSTER/VICE PRESIDENT OF MANHATTAN INSTITUTE: Yes. Well, I mean, donors are giving through different vehicles. A lot of donors have been giving historically to some of these big ideological groups that have driven, you know, I think the Democratic Party further to the left -- right? -- as more of these groups are sort of organizing around the same causes.

CORNISH: But you mean sort of like the way they'd be, like, Club for Growth, do you say this? And now the money is going to something not quite the same.

CORNISH: Not as ideological. ARM: Actually, I do think they are saying increasingly the same thing.

ARM: I'm seeing a lot of ads from clients, a lot of communications on social media from Climate Defiance that are about issues in the Middle East.

Ditto a lot of the big abortion groups have all kind of consolidated on one sort of omni cause message.

I think a lot of our problems in our politics right now are downstream from the fact that on the right, you've sort of got one guy who's in charge, who's a boss, and a lot of ideological diversity that's allowed to work around his orbit, so long as you kiss that ring and then over on the left, no one who's necessarily in charge. But everyone's swimming in the same direction ideologically.

The mainstream Democrats, like the Haley Stevens of the party, haven't really been able to run effective campaigns against the more radical flank, because they're not willing to say what they're for that the DSA left is against. That's been a real challenge for Haley Stevens.

Look, Rashida Tlaib, the congresswoman from Michigan, is hitting Haley Stevens, because she's got support from General Motors and General Mills.

CORNISH: But can I interrupt with those --

ARM: Those are big Michigan companies.

CORNISH: I understand that. But also, Michigan has been a canary. Right? And its car factory for like a couple of years now. I mean, ever since October 7th.

And I remember the Biden administration trying to find a way to talk about Gaza and Israel with an electorate. And it had nothing in common with that electorate anymore. And Michigan was the place where I remember the DNC. Their electors were the most frustrated. Right?

That's where you really -- it felt like that was the place that had this dialog the most strongly. And it feels almost inevitable that you'd see a candidate like Abdullah el-Sayed come forward.

ROCHA: And I think that's why you see the UAW endorsed him. I talked to somebody at the UAW this morning early, and they told me that they have talked to 120,000 of their active and retired members. And they make up 9 percent of the early vote, because they can take the data that we get back from the elections on who has voted early and cross match it against their voter files of their members.

That's crazy good for them. But again, to your point, it's because it's Michigan. You've seen a downturn in manufacturing. You have this very diverse electorate, and you see a lot of the economics coming to Michigan. And that's why you see that.

CORNISH: I want to show you guys one more thing. Their supporters, who they've gotten endorsements from.

So, when you look at Haley Stevens, she's gotten the governor, Senator Chuck Schumer. And then when you look at Abdul el-Sayed, you've got Bernie Sanders, AOC, Elizabeth Warren.

And that -- that last group of three, I feel like this has been percolating for a while, right? In terms of long-term movements percolating in the party.

ARM: Well, one thing that's worth mentioning and responding to is that the UAW, at a national level, is now 25 percent, more than that, graduate students. OK? So, this isn't your father's UAW.

And Haley Stevens has the support of a lot of the big manufacturing unions that are constituted at a national level, more of actual workers at that level. So --

CORNISH: So, you mean non-unions? Or what do you mean by that?

ARM: I think graduate students are part of what's driving the UAW farther to the left.

CORNISH: No, I mean when you said what's supporting her? You're saying it's --

ARM: Haley Stevens has the support of a number of other unions in the state.

CORNISH: That you see as more worker-oriented or not having the --

CORNISH: -- one in four graduate --

ARM: I mean, I think Abdullah El-Sayed is winning, because he's running a virulently anti-Israel campaign, as you said, Audie.

I don't think it's because he's talking about bringing manufacturing back to Michigan. That's what Haley Stevens has been talking about. In fact, it's kind of the only thing she can talk about.

CORNISH: Let me underscore, I did not say he was running a virulently anti-Israel campaign.

CORNISH: I want you to own your comments.

ARM: I don't think -- I don't think he -- I don't think he --

CORNISH: Just so you can get credit for your own comments.

ARM: I did think he would dispute that he's running a virulently anti- Israel campaign. CORNISH: I would dispute I said it.

And I want to give the last word to Aaron, because Bernie Sanders, when I think of him grumpy with his arms crossed at that DNC many years ago.

BLAKE: With the mittens on, yes.

CORNISH: Elizabeth Warren, it feels like we are seeing the fruits of a long-running movement that may or may not be coming to fruition.

BLAKE: Yes. And this is a very big moment for that movement. And I'll tell you why. The reason is because the Democratic primary electorate has proven willing to elect these kinds of candidates. The DSA candidates in -- in cities like New York City, in cities, you know, heavily urban areas.

CORNISH: And only now.

BLAKE: In between Boulder in Colorado. They haven't gotten these candidates, necessarily, through primaries in marquee races, in swing electorates.

So, getting Abdul el-Sayed through this primary and having him tested in a general election that is going to have lots of focus in November, is a big moment for this movement. They need to prove that they can win in that kind of environment, not just primaries, but general elections with swing electorates. And that's why I think this race is so important for that movement.

CORNISH: All right. So, big test. That's why we're watching it.

I want to turn to something else on CNN THIS MORNING. The ethics panel that wants to censure Republican Chuck Edwards. We're going to talk about why some women in the House of Representatives say that is not enough.

And then today, the White House will meet with leaders in A.I. Will we finally get the guardrails that have been promised?

And Ariana Grande speaking out in her own words. Why she is stepping away from the spotlight.

CORNISH: OK, it's now 15 minutes past the hour. Here are five things making the news this morning.

That multi-state cyclosporiasis outbreak has turned deadly. Two people in Michigan have died from the intestinal illness, which causes dramatic stomach upset and can lead to severe dehydration. Officials say both victims had underlying health conditions.

At this point, more than 18,000 cases have been reported in the U.S. And former special counsel Jack Smith, willing to testify publicly

before a Senate committee. That's according to a letter from his attorneys to Chairman Chuck Grassley, obtained by CNN.

Now, Grassley had asked him to testify on September 22nd, if approved by the Justice Department.

Smith is facing scrutiny over his investigation into President Trump's alleged attempts to overthrow the 2020 election and his use of subpoenas to obtain lawmakers' text messages as part of that investigation.

And later today, the White House is going to meet with the leaders of artificial intelligence companies about a new framework for government oversight.

Now, it's expected to include provisions to voluntarily allow the government to review new models before they release them. And the meeting comes just before -- just before both. Sorry. Just after both OpenAI and Anthropic reported incidents of an A.I. agent going rogue and hacking into competitor companies.

Now, the FAA is investigating a near miss in Florida after a small training plane lost engine power and then landed directly on the interstate.

Audio captures the moment the pilot warned that they wouldn't make it to the airport's runway.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: We are not making the airport. We're going down on I-10. Tower, can you still hear for Number 62?

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Number 62, I've got you loud and clear. What do you need?

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE: I just want to let you know we are lined up with I-10, trying to avoid the cars.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Number 62. Roger, we're going to get everybody over there as fast as they can to help you out.

CORNISH: And then this is dash cam video from a truck showing the plane nearly missing a highway sign.

And Ariana Grande addressing rumors in a speech to the crowd on her Chicago tour stop last night. She confirmed that she is taking a step back from public life.

The singer has been under intense scrutiny for her appearance, especially after her new album and its music video dropped last week.

So, what she told fans last night is that her decision is not reactive, and it's something that has been planned for some time.

Now, after the break on CNN THIS MORNING, the Justice Department admits it was a botched renovation that caused the issues with the Reflecting Pool, not vandalism. But that's not what the president wanted to hear.

So, who might lose their jobs because of this?

Today, the Senate Judiciary Committee is going to vote on Todd Blanche's nomination for A.G. Does he have the votes for a new gig?

In the meantime, good morning to our viewers in New York City. A look at the sunrise over the skyline.

DONALD TRUMP, U.S. PRESIDENT: Jeanine Pirro made a mistake. There was vandalism.

Frankly, I think she choked. She choked. I don't know what the hell happened.

I was disappointed with Jeanine Pirro. Really disappointed with Jeanine Pirro. She -- she folded like an umbrella.

CORNISH: OK. After weeks of algae blooms and chipping bottoms, President Trump furious at his longtime ally, Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney in D.C., over the pool vandalism case.

So, you've got sources telling CNN that he stopped short of firing her during a White House meeting on Monday. But he did, obviously, lash out at her, because the Justice Department admitted the pool problems were caused by a flawed renovation rather than vandalism, as the president has long claimed.

Now, her office also said it's dropping the criminal case against the man accused of being the so-called vandal. He was an Olympian, David Hearn.

And the Justice Department acknowledged in a court filing that the $14 million renovation was hasty and botched.

Just last month, Pirro was saying something different.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Did he have any tools, or was it just his bare hands?

JEANINE PIRRO, U.S. ATTORNEY IN WASHINGTON D.C.: Right now, we believe it's his bare hands. Both hands.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Does that indicate, in your belief, that it was probably damaged before, or do you believe that he --

PIRRO: Oh, he damaged it.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Further. But do you believe it had already been damaged before?

PIRRO: He damaged the pool.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: Before he touched it?

PIRRO: He damaged this pool.

CORNISH: Group chat is back. So, we were talking during the break. This filing is stunning. I know people have been talking about it for a couple of days.

But what I don't understand is Trump lashing out at Pirro. Why do you think she has come in for such criticism from him when she has gone after just about everyone, you know, that he has been frustrated with?

BLAKE: Yes, I mean, look, Trump is somebody who certainly expects loyalty from the people around him. He wants them to hew to his theory of the case.

And in this case, the theory of the case was that -- that there was vandalism, even though there wasn't any real public reason to believe that.

The problem is that we've seen this over and over again, over the last 18 months or so; is that when these theories actually have to be tested in court, that doesn't go very well. Because there are standards of evidence. There are representations.

CORNISH: While you're talking, can I show you some headlines? Because we were looking at this. The number of cases: Minnesota protesters, right? Hurdles there in getting those arrests to charges right now.

Justice Department drops its "New York Times" subpoena.

California, the labor leader.

I'm actually keeping a running list on my desk in office of cases that people have been arrested. The charges don't go anywhere.

What's going on with the Justice Department? Or is the weaponization the point? Putting people through the frustration of arrests and all of that to kind of get rid of them or be a nuisance?

ARM: I mean, I do think it's, you know, nice to see that this administration is responsive to the courts. There was a lot of hemming and hawing about the fact that Donald Trump would not abide by the decisions of the Supreme Court or other courts at any point.

This administration is operating within the confines of the law and operating like it is bound to the law.

CORNISH: So, they take the "L," you're saying? They're not trying to override the system, like -- or the system is working?

ARM: Well, we'll see. I mean, we'll see what they do, right? I mean, he could theoretically fire Jeanine Pirro for this. I wouldn't necessarily be enthusiastic about that.

I think this is someone who's been a pretty good soldier for the president and his administration. You know, has been -- has a job that's bigger than the Reflecting Pool, right?

ARM: Has been involved in these efforts to clean up and crack down on crime in D.C.

CORNISH: And seen a lot of those cases flop, as well. This has been kind of interesting.

ROCHA: I think Donald Trump runs under the old East Texas philosophy of, if you lie long enough about having a horse, eventually somebody will buy you a saddle.

He's not used to telling the truth, and he don't like to be told he's wrong.

Remember the guy who went to Congress this week or last week, who wants a big job, who couldn't say that Joe Biden won the election because folks are scared to death to cross him?

And Jeanine Pirro, he thinks, just did that. And he don't like that at all.

CORNISH: Did she really cross him? What do you think is going on legally in that office?

Because that filing not only said this was a botched renovation job, it said there's no way this guy reached into the middle of the pool with his bare hands, unless it was, like, one of the Fantastic Four. None of this makes sense.

We did not say this. The Interior Department said this. I mean, they threw another department under the bus.

CORNISH: It was -- in its totality, it said this didn't happen.

BLAKE: This -- this document read like some lawyers at the Justice Department, who were tired of dealing with this case and wanted to just get it out there and -- and wash their hands of it.

It is a remarkable document, because you're right. It's not just saying, oh, the evidence isn't quite there. It's basically pointing the finger at another department of the administration and saying that department withheld evidence from us that allowed us to move forward with a case that could have put somebody in prison wrongfully.

Basically, that's the -- the logical extent of what they put out.

BLAKE: And I think that, in any other time, if, you know -- when Democrats take over the -- the House, if they do in January, this is the kind of thing that you would want to have congressional hearings and issue subpoenas.

CORNISH: The paperwork comes back. Yes, because it also points to the contractor and also points to -- it says it in here, that the contractor was rushing to meet the America 250 deadline.

And it was, like, this is a lot to be putting in here for people to look at later and raise questions about.

ARM: Yes, I mean, I don't think it's an inherently bad thing that you had a contractor who was rushing to meet a deadline to try and clean up D.C. ahead of America 250.

Obviously, if you're going after the wrong person, that's a bigger problem.

But look, it's not the first time, and it won't be the last time that an administration looks to pursue a case that it knows it probably can't win in court.

We had with the Biden administration, right? They attempted to wipe all student debt until the Supreme Court came along and said, actually, you can't really do that. But Joe Biden's staffers saw --

CORNISH: But each one of these is someone taking the time, doing the evidentiary work, going to court. It costs money.

CORNISH: The Reflecting Pool costs money. Pretty soon, it starts to cost money.

And at what point, if you're running a business and you're a businessperson, do you look around and say, I'm just -- this is creating problems. It's costing money. It's not working. And is that something that the voter starts to get frustrated with?

ROCHA: We've talked a lot about cost and corruption as we move into the midterms, and the thing that we're not talking about is we keep talking about this contractor.

We've reported on this network that the contract was somebody that worked on a pool down at Mar-a-Lago. We have said that. Now, I'm not saying any wrongdoing was done. But it looks like --

CORNISH: Yes. The question of no-bid, et cetera.

ROCHA: Right. The no-bid contract stuff, and now it still ain't fixed. And it's cost how much money? Like I ain't running a TV commercial on this in the midterms. But it's just another thing that stacks up.

ARM: Well, that's the key point. I don't think any undecided voters are going to be making their decision based on Reflecting Pool dynamics.

ROCHA: But it's just one more thing. Right.

Today: Voters Head To Polls In Michigan Senate Race; Former Trump Official Files Restraining Order Against Rep. Miller. Aired 6:30-7a ET

Aired August 04, 2026 - 06:30   ET

THIS IS A RUSH TRANSCRIPT. THIS COPY MAY NOT BE IN ITS FINAL FORM AND MAY BE UPDATED.

CHUCK ROCHA, DEMOCRATIC STRATEGIST: -- running a TV commercial on this in the midterms.

But it's just another thing that stacks up.

JESSE ARM, POLLSTER: Well, that's the key point. I don't think any undecided voters are going to be making their decision based on reflecting pool dynamics.

AUDIE CORNISH, CNN ANCHOR: Got it. Okay.

Straight ahead on CNN THIS MORNING, Michigan's primary shines a light on the deep divide in the Democratic Party and ask whether voters are choosing an ideology or candidate they think can win in November. Plus, crews scrambling to gain control on wildfires in Washington state as the weather turns dangerous again.

CORNISH: Good morning, everybody. I'm Audie Cornish. Thank you for joining me on CNN THIS MORNING.

It is half past the hour. And here's what's happening right now.

In Washington, a man is arrested on arson charges in connection with one of three wildfires burning in the state. The 37-year-old man is being held on a $1 million bond, and officials say the fires are expected to keep burning for weeks. Already, more than 65,000 people have been forced from their homes.

And in just a few hours, the Senate Judiciary Committee will vote on Todd Blanche's nomination for attorney general. The first vote was delayed last week due to concerns from two key Republicans, but both have signaled they will vote yes after Blanche formally rescinded the presidents $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund.

And happening now, polls are set to open for critical primary elections in five key states. Michigan, Missouri, Kansas, Virginia and Washington. Today's races will settle nominations in the Senate, House and gubernatorial races as we get closer to the midterms this November.

And one of today's most closely watched contests is Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. It's a key test of where the party is headed. There's Haley Stevens making her final campaign pitch, framing herself as the pragmatic choice to take on Republican Mike Rogers in November.

Meanwhile, Abdul El-Sayed rallied Detroit progressives and mounted a direct challenge to the party's Washington establishment.

ABDUL EL-SAYED (D), MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE; I believe in what we're going to do. I believe in the opportunity we have in front of us to take our democracy back from the likes of the corporations and the billionaires and the special interests who want to tell us what we cannot have and should not fight for.

REP. HALEY STEVENS (D), MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE: West Michigan needs a senator who's going to deliver, who's going to show up, who's going to show you that I can campaign like I govern and I govern like I campaign, I'm present, I'm focused, I'm dedicated.

CORNISH: Joining me now, two journalists who have been following these candidates closely. Dana Milbank, political columnist for "NOTUS", and Nicholas Wu, congressional reporter for "Semafor".

Let me start with my congressional reporter. I know you like to cover the House, so it must be so irritating to be stuck covering the Senate. What is it about this race that you think is making it kind of one of the most written about?

NICHOLAS WU, CONGRESSIONAL REPORTER, SEMAFOR: Well, this is one of the clearest ideological divides were seeing in pretty much any Senate race in the country in the primary. Since we have such a clear division between the folks who have lined up behind Abdul El-Sayed, progressives, AOC, Bernie Sanders and so on.

CORNISH: And put up their endorsements so people can see that pretty clearly. Haley stevens got Chuck Schumer, Gretchen Whitmer. It is -- it's pretty obvious if you were drawing, if you asked a kid to draw a picture of wings of the party, these are the faces that would be on opposite sides.

WU: Exactly. And beyond that, you have very clear ideological divides when it comes to Israel, which, you know, in our post-October 7th environment has become such a huge dividing line among Democrats as they look to build the future of their party.

CORNISH: How come you say this is not a civil war? You've been writing about this, and it sounds like you think it's overblown. DANA MILBANK, POLITICAL COLUMNIST, NOTUS: I mean, what Nick is saying

is all true. I think some of it is a little overblown. I mean, one of the main reasons El-Sayed is doing so well is he's just extremely charismatic. I mean, he's a very good politician, you know?

And for all the talk of divisions within the Democratic Party, the electorate is actually pretty close. You know, it's probably more unified than it's been really in decades. And you see, you know, even the mainstream of the party, the so-called establishment, has gone substantially to the left in recent years. So, yeah, there's this huge divide they have on Israel, but the whole party is moving in El-Sayed direction on Israel.

They're both looking for universal health care, just different ways of getting there.

MILBANK: So a lot of --

CORNISH: It comes down to that dreaded word electability. Here's what Abdul El-Sayed said about that when he was asked on CNN on Sunday.

JEFF ZELENY, CNN CHIEF NATIONAL AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT: How much of this is about convincing people that you can win in November?

EL-SAYED: The question of can I win in November is, is a question that voters alone can answer. Convincing folks like you and everybody who watches from everywhere else, I'm so sorry. It just doesn't matter.

Electability is the thing that's best defined after the fact. So -- if and when I get elected, then you'll know I'm electable.

CORNISH: I feel like Donald Trump, it applied to him, right? Like for the longest time, all I heard from Republicans is this guy is not a Republican. This isn't serious. Some of the people in his cabinet, some of the people who are with him now were people who said he was not electable. And here we are.

And so, I'm wondering if we're at the beginning of a movement that ends with some version of that for Democrats, someone that they thought was not electable, who suddenly is.

MILBANK: Yeah, I'm not sure that he's wrong in making this electability argument. The populist appeal that he has is really considerable. You know, you don't hear a word out of his mouth about sort of the woke issues, the cultural issues, and it's all pocketbook economic issues. So I'm sure --

CORNISH: But I think those issues can be pretty much foisted on you when you get to a general election, right? Like everything that Mamdani is doing in New York becomes the thing that everyone else has to run against.

MILBANK: Right. I mean, the conventional wisdom is Mike Rogers is very delighted to have El-Sayed as his opponent, but it's not entirely clear that that's the case.

MILBANK: He can ignite a populist fire. And that's what will be interesting in the fall.

CORNISH: Let me play one more thing for you. It's the vote I always keep an eye on in states like this. This is the Reverend Dr. Charles William II on CNN. This was on Sunday.

REV. DR. CHARLES WILLIAMS II, SENIOR PASTOR, HISTORIC KING SOLOMON BAPTIST CHURCH: She's the only one in the race that's actually been elected. She was elected a congressperson. She worked in the executive branch.

And of course, she has been a legislator. She understands how to work to get policy passed. Unfortunately, there's nobody else in the race at this time that has that cache.

CORNISH: Historic King Solomon Church. There is always that Black Church vote that comes out, and they aren't always aligned with the academic progressive left vote. We see this in South Carolina. Biden was happy to receive those votes.

Is that the kind of thing that's a wild card here in Michigan, or are those voters also embracing some of these more populist ideas or ideas on foreign policy?

WU: I mean, the strategy that the Stevens campaign is running is to try to run up turnout in Black majority areas in Michigan. Whether that is --

CORNISH: I think I saw her at a church.

WU: Exactly. Right. Right.

CORNISH: The obligatory many times Democrats, Black church visit. That happens.

WU: Exactly. She's been trying to run up turnout there. El-Sayed has been trying to cut into those margins. For example, you know, we saw him going around Detroit with a whole crew of influencers. So it's like it's a much different kind of strategy --

CORNISH: Very different reach, but I understand.

WU: Exactly. MILBANK: And the polling shows him ahead, but it's just sort of a

guess by the pollsters about is it going to be young male white voters? Is it going to be older female black voters? We don't really know until tonight or tomorrow.

CORNISH: Yeah. Both are frustrated for different reasons. And there's always the couch, as it's said, right.

You guys, thank you so much. Hope to have you back in the group.

And tonight, don't miss key primary races across the country, including big gubernatorial and congressional races, as we've talked about of Michigan. We're going to talk about who's going to advance and we're going to have election results all night.

You can get that tonight on CNN and our CNN app.

Next on CNN THIS MORNING, a Republican lawmaker facing censure after an ethics report showing that he gave female staffers jewelry, vacations and guns. But some don't think that punishment goes far enough.

Plus, I'm going to talk to a reporter who sat down with Congressman Max Miller. What he told her about the abuse allegations he's facing.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I know Max. He's a -- he's a good person. I mean, I always thought he was a very good person. And I'm going to let the families figure that out. But it's accusations, and I'm going to let them figure that out.

CORNISH: President Trump publicly standing by embattled Republican Congressman Max Miller, even as his former press secretary launches a new legal battle against Miller.

So, on Monday, Stephanie Grisham's lawyer filed for a temporary restraining order against Miller. Now she's suing him for breaking the terms of a nondisclosure agreement, an agreement that stems from 2021. In a "Washington Post" op-ed, Grisham had written about abuse allegations dealing with an ex-boyfriend, and Miller sued her at the time, but they settled out of court and agreed not to disparage each other publicly.

Grisham now claims Miller violated the deal in this interview back in June.

REP. MAX MILLER (R-OH): Without question, every allegation should be taken seriously. What should be noted is that allegation came out on the same day as somebody's book launch.

And the other part, what I would like to discuss is my ex-wife was with me every single day during that time of my life, in that election. And she, in her own words, will tell you that I never did any of those things. And she never saw evidence of me ever doing those things. And that was nothing more than somebody trying to get notoriety.

CORNISH: Joining the group chat, Harri Leigh, political correspondent at Spectrum News. She conducted that interview with Congressman Miller.

This is a fascinating conversation that you got to have with him. Before we get to the allegations within his family and ex-wife, can you talk about this issue with Stephanie Grisham, why they are all of a sudden back in court?

HARRI LEIGH, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT, SPECTRUM NEWS: Well, they're back in court partly because of that interview and their nondisclosure agreement back in 2021. It appears this was a confidential agreement. So we didn't know until she filed this suit.

But it appears that they agreed not to disparage each other. And she's saying that in that interview, by denying the claims that she made, as well as the claims by his now ex-wife, that he broke that agreement. And as you know, yesterday she also filed a restraining order.

CORNISH: Right. Because he's basically saying there are not multiple allegations, right? He doesn't want this to sound like it's piling up. And so, he reached back to this conversation and she's like, no, keep me out of it.

CORNISH: All right. So, let's talk about the Moreno family. The Senator Bernie Moreno has been obviously, like, very upset and frustrated. He has called for Miller to step down, saying he shouldn't be in Congress anymore.

Joining him, Senator Shelley Moore Capito and Roger Marshall.

Are we going to see any other senators speak up?

ARM: I think Rick Scott might have said something to that effect. Yeah, I don't know.

CORNISH: When does it reach the House? The people who actually work with this guy?

AARON BLAKE, CNN SENIOR POLITICAL REPORER: I think it's getting to that point now. We're seeing signals coming out of the White House where at least Trump is apparently privately saying that he doesn't think Max Miller can win reelection.

That seems like the beginnings of kind of a subtle pressure campaign to convince this person to at least step aside from his reelection campaign. And there's a very good reason for that. You know, even besides from -- aside from kind of the details of the allegations, this is a district that Republicans would worry about losing if Max Miller is on the ballot in November. That's the same with some of these other congressmen, which were talking about.

CORNISH: But now, we're talking about family. So, for instance, Senator Moreno, like I said, he put out a statement where he says, as he admitted privately, Max Miller needs serious psychological help. He's a danger to my daughter. I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter.

And then there is also this audio obtained from earlier this year. Emily Moreno is telling police about an incident on New Year's Eve where she alleged that Miller held a gun to her head when she was changing their infant daughter. So just give you a moment to listen to this.

OFFICER: So when -- when does the gun come into play?

EMILY MORENO, EX-WIFE: When I'm changing (AUDIO DELETED).

OFFICER: And what does he do?

MORENO: Holds it on me.

OFFICER: Holds it on you? Okay, can you show me where he held it to you?

No, hey, it's -- it's okay, that's fine, that's fine. Like I said, I -- that's a hard thing to talk about.

CORNISH: Has he said anything about this incident or others? Because I know he released his own drop box of audio. So, he does want people to kind of hear his side as he's denying these allegations.

LEIGH: Yeah. And I think that's part of the problem is that he keeps releasing more and more information and more evidence that can then be used against him in certain cases. He does deny that this incident even happened.

CORNISH: What does he say about his father in law? Has he talked about what's going on publicly?

LEIGH; So, for a long time he said that they could work together. He said that he could walk and chew gum at the same time. But after a while, he was saying that his father-in-law was helping his daughter, enabling her in what he said was lying. And so that is when he started taking to social media to criticize

him. Bernie Moreno didn't say anything for a very long time. His team consistently said no comment until Sunday, and that is when he released that scathing post on X.

CORNISH: And then he was asked about it. I just want to play some video of the last time Moreno was asked about this incident. Oh, sorry about that. It is actually a full screen. I'm not sure I can say it because it involves swearing.

It says, you know, I hope you never have to go through a situation like this and you wouldn't ask that kind of effing question.

And I think it's a great example of the fact that they do want this not to be so public. This isn't something that they want to be discussed this way. Do you think it would be discussed this way if it weren't two lawmakers involved?

ROCHA: Yeah, I think we'd be having a whole different conversation. We'd also be doing it different if Bernie Moreno wasn't just elected, that means he's not up for reelection. Everybody at home should know. Just because you're a senator don't mean you're up for elections every six years.

Just elected. He's not up for another four and a half years for reelection. But in the house, to your point. Audie, everybody is up every two years. And in this congressional race, it's only an R plus seven, which should be a very safe seat. And in most circumstances, it would be a very safe seat.

But when you put that on the screen, an ad maker like me can run that against -- he's running against an ironworker, a regular union guy, and that makes that be more vulnerable.

That's why you have to put politics in this horrible situation where you're talking about guns and babies, which nobody should live through.

CORNISH: All right, so let's turn to that. Another Huse Republican facing ethics scrutiny. The ethics committee is recommending a full vote to censure North Carolina's Chuck Edwards, a months-long probe found that Edwards engaged in persistent, inappropriate conduct toward two young female staffers. That's from the ethics panel report.

Now, examples that they provided included skipping scheduled house votes to help a staffer decorate her Christmas tree, writing and reading a tearful personal poem at a staffers departure party and buying a staffer lavish gifts, including jewelry worth more than $1,000.

Edwards and his team reject the allegations. They claim that the ethics committee failed to demonstrate that either of the two staffers actually expressed discomfort to Edwards regarding his conduct with them.

The group chat is back. I wanted to follow up with this because just a few weeks ago, Mike

Johnson was saying, I want to ban dating, not just of your own staffers, but across the board. So, obviously, there was like a Houston, we have a problem situation.

What do you see in the fact that there's a censure going on here, but that hasn't come up yet with Moreno.

CORNISH: With Miller. Sorry.

LEIGH: I think that they've -- they've expressed some issues with due process. I think that now that the ethics investigation is over with Edwards, they feel more comfortable moving forward with that. But we have seen several lawmakers refuse to take a stand until the Ethics Committee makes a decision.

I don't actually know if they have started that yet, but --

CORNISH: And I'm going to throw up on screen so people can see the number of lawmakers who are facing some kind of sexual harassment or ethics investigation at this point.

And one of the people in the past was Jorge Santos. And it was interesting. I remember thinking, Jorge Santos is not going to have to leave Congress unless a Democrat also is a problem, and they can be asked to leave Congress. Like there seemed to be a kind of one for one situation that had to happen.

Is that the case right now? Just the balance of power is so tight that leadership is loathe to let anyone go?

ROCHA: That's the point here. I mean, I think that's exactly what's happening.

CORNISH: But even for Democrats, you can be like on your deathbed and still in Congress.

ROCHA: Absolutely. And you can die in office if you stay there until you're 90. I mean, it's just one thing after another.

And I think this is where the American people are fed up with both parties. When you say, what do you think about Democrats? What do you think about Republicans? You're like, well, they're all too old, and they're all a bunch of crooks that seem like they\re acting like a bunch of freaks on Capitol Hill.

ARM: I genuinely weird behavior from Edwards's part.

ARM: From Edwards's part.

ARM: I mean, that's the latest one you've raised, Audie. I just -- it is strange to me that, you know, even if it is true what his office is saying, that none of these people ever complained about this, that one would think it's appropriate to shower young female staffers and these kinds of gifts and invite them to things, it's just, you know, it's strange.

CORNISH: Yeah, which two adult -- two consenting adults outside of this environment? Sure. But you know what I mean? But in Congress, there has been this sense that there's some other standard. And is that dead?

ARM: I think there is some credit that is actually due here to Speaker Johnson, who I would say probably saying nobody who works in Congress can date anybody else who works in Congress is maybe a little bit of an overcorrection. I'm not sure if that's exactly what he proposed, but if it is, I would say that, you know, maybe a bit heavy handed, but look, it's a -- it's a House Republican majority. And that ethics committee is the one that dealt down this decision.

CORNISH: Right, it's Republicans leading that committee. Yeah.

ARM: Edwards. So, you know, I respect the fact and appreciate that there is at least an effort here to clean up house and recognition that there is a problem.

ROCHA: And if Democrats take the House, which they probably will, at least in the house, it'd be interesting to watch how they deal -- how they deal with the ethics committee on either side.

CORNISH: I know, because they also always complain about the ethics committee. That's like a big Democrat thing. They're always frustrated with.

Since you were here, we want to give you something positive to talk about what is in your group chat other than people being like, oh my God, did you talk to this lawmaker? How did that interview go? What are people talking about in your world?

LEIGH: That's been a big thing this week, I'm going to say. But I think, you know, we're talking a lot about how the House, the Senate are going out. They leave so much unfinished business, so much that did not get passed. And it's going to be such a rush when they come back in September. Just talking about the budget, the NDAA, the crypto bill, military funding. So --

CORNISH: The military funding, even?

LEIGH: All the NDAA.

CORNISH: Yeah. You think that's not going to get done this week?
